```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96)
library(covassistedGM)
sup <- system.file("original_supplement", package = "covassistedGM")
load_sup <- function(f) { e <- new.env(); load(file.path(sup, "RData", f), envir = e); as.list(e) }
```

Section 4 of Niu et al. (2024) has three simulation studies. Each is generated by a
`simulate_example*()` function that is the data block of the corresponding script, so with
the paper's seed the data are identical to the authors'. The MCMC runs of the paper take
minutes to hours; this vignette runs short chains live and loads the authors' saved results
(shipped in `inst/original_supplement/RData`) for the figures, saying in each case which is
which. The scripts `inst/scripts/Example*_package.R` run everything at full length.

## Example 1: piecewise linear precision matrix (3 nodes)

A scalar covariate on three intervals; on each interval a different 3-node graph whose
non-zero precision entries are linear in $x$. The PxG model with the Gaussian / G-Wishart
specification is compared with the covariate-only and graph-only models by DIC, and with the
kernel graphical lasso (k-lasso) by mean squared error of the partial correlations.

```{r ex1-data}
sim1 <- simulate_example1(seed = 2020)
str(sim1[c("Y", "X")])
```

The authors' call (`burnin = 500`, `nmcmc = 1000`) and their reported DIC values:

```{r ex1-fit, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(2020)
A <- PxG_GW(Y = sim1$Y, X = sim1$X, b = 3, D = diag(3), alphaG = 0.1,
            mu0 = 0, sigsq0 = 1, b1 = 1, b2 = 1, M = 1, N = 5,
            burnin = 500, nmcmc = 1000, z0 = sample(1:15, 300, TRUE), B = 1)   # DIC 2193.304
set.seed(2020)
B <- CovOnly_GW(Y = sim1$Y, X = sim1$X, b = 3, D = diag(3), alphaG = 0.1,
                mu0 = 0, sigsq0 = 1, b1 = 1, b2 = 1, M = 1, N = 5,
                burnin = 500, nmcmc = 1000, z0 = sample(1:15, 300, TRUE), B = 1) # DIC 2584.573
set.seed(2020)
C <- GraphOnly_GW(Y = sim1$Y, X = sim1$X, b = 3, D = diag(3), alphaG = 0.1,
                  mu0 = 0, sigsq0 = 1, b1 = 1, b2 = 1, M = 1, N = 5,
                  burnin = 500, nmcmc = 1000, z0 = sample(1:15, 300, TRUE), B = 1) # DIC 3189.946
```

Note that `z0 = sample(1:15, 300, TRUE)` with `N = 5` is what the script does: labels above
5 are simply empty clusters until the first allocation sweep. The saved results:

```{r ex1-saved}
A <- load_sup("Example1A.RData")$A; B <- load_sup("Example1B.RData")$B; C <- load_sup("Example1C.RData")$C
c(PxG = A$DIC, covariate_only = B$DIC, graph_only = C$DIC)
table(PxG_label = A$Label, interval = rep(1:3, each = 100))
```

Figure 3 plots the posterior edge inclusion probability of each edge against $x$ (lowess
smoothed, as in the script) over the true step function:

```{r ex1-fig3, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 9}
xseq <- seq(-1, 1, by = 0.01)
truth <- function(i, j) sapply(xseq, function(v) sim1$G0(if (v < -1/3) 1 else if (v > 1/3) 3 else 2, v)[i, j])
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2, 1))
for (e in list(c(1, 2), c(1, 3), c(2, 3))) {
  plot(xseq, truth(e[1], e[2]), type = "l", ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "x", ylab = bquote(p[.(paste0(e[1], e[2]))]))
  lines(lowess(sim1$x, A$Gsum[e[1], e[2], ], f = 0.3), col = "red")
}
legend("bottomright", c("true edge", "PxG posterior"), col = c("black", "red"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

Figure 4 does the same for the partial correlations, against k-lasso. The k-lasso fit takes
about 100 minutes in the authors' loop; its saved result is loaded.

```{r ex1-fig4, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 9}
K <- load_sup("klasso.RData")$Omega_est
true_pc <- function(i, j) sapply(seq_along(sim1$x), function(s) {
  v <- sim1$x[s]; sim1$Omega(if (s <= 100) 1 else if (s <= 200) 2 else 3, v)[i, j] / 1.2 })
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2, 1))
mse <- matrix(NA, 3, 2, dimnames = list(c("12", "13", "23"), c("PxG", "k-lasso")))
for (r in 1:3) {
  e <- list(c(1, 2), c(1, 3), c(2, 3))[[r]]
  pxg <- partial_correlation_path(A, e[1], e[2])
  kl <- K[e[1], e[2], ] / sqrt(K[e[1], e[1], ] * K[e[2], e[2], ])
  tr <- true_pc(e[1], e[2])
  mse[r, ] <- c(mean((pxg - tr)^2), mean((kl - tr)^2))
  plot(sim1$x, tr, type = "l", ylim = c(-0.2, 1), xlab = "x", ylab = bquote(rho[.(paste0(e[1], e[2]))]))
  lines(lowess(sim1$x, pxg, f = 0.3), col = "red"); lines(lowess(sim1$x, kl, f = 0.3), col = "blue")
}
legend("topright", c("truth", "PxG", "k-lasso"), col = c("black", "red", "blue"), lty = 1, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
round(mse, 4)
```

The paper reports MSEs of 0.0251, 0.0221 and 0.0104 for PxG against 0.1433, 0.1094 and
0.2266 for k-lasso (the script's third k-lasso value compares edge 1-2 with the truth of edge
2-3, so the table above, which uses edge 2-3 for both, differs in that cell).

A live short chain, to show the function running:

```{r ex1-live}
set.seed(2020)
A_short <- PxG_GW(Y = sim1$Y, X = sim1$X, b = 3, D = diag(3), alphaG = 0.1,
                  mu0 = 0, sigsq0 = 1, b1 = 1, b2 = 1, M = 1, N = 5,
                  burnin = 20, nmcmc = 60, z0 = sample(1:15, 300, TRUE), B = 1, verbose = FALSE)
table(A_short$Label, rep(1:3, each = 100))
```

## Example 2: linear precision matrix with a constant graph (5 nodes)

Here the graph is the same chain 1-2-3-4-5 for every sample but every non-zero partial
correlation equals $x/1.4$, so methods that assume a common precision matrix (BM13, mSSL)
cannot describe the data while PxG approximates the linear trend with a staircase of
clusters.

```{r ex2}
sim2 <- simulate_example2(seed = 2020)
A2 <- load_sup("Example2.RData")$A
table(A2$Label)
```

```{r ex2-fig5, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 10}
par(mfrow = c(1, 4), mar = c(4.5, 4.5, 2, 1))
truerho <- sim2$x / 1.4
for (e in list(c(1, 2), c(2, 3), c(3, 4), c(4, 5))) {
  est <- partial_correlation_path(A2, e[1], e[2])
  o <- order(sim2$x)
  plot(sim2$x[o], truerho[o], type = "l", xlab = "x", ylab = bquote(rho[.(paste0(e[1], e[2]))]), ylim = c(-0.7, 0.7))
  lines(lowess(sim2$x, est, f = 0.4), col = "red")
  legend("topleft", sprintf("MSE %.4f", mean((est - truerho)^2)), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}
```

The paper's MSEs for the four edges are 0.0077, 0.0078, 0.0078 and 0.0125. The comparison
with BM13 and mSSL (Figure 6) is in `vignette("competitors")`.

## Example 3: two clusters, 50 nodes, 10 covariates

Two equal groups of 250 samples whose covariates differ in mean (0 versus 2) and whose
50-node graphs are independent sparse random graphs with G-Wishart precision matrices. This
is the first example that uses the pseudo-likelihood sampler in C++.

```{r ex3}
sim3 <- simulate_example3(seed = 2022)
c(edges_G1 = (sum(sim3$G1) - 50) / 2, edges_G2 = (sum(sim3$G2) - 50) / 2)
A3 <- load_sup("Example3A.RData")$A; B3 <- load_sup("Example3B.RData")$B; C3 <- load_sup("Example3C.RData")$C
c(PxG = A3$DIC, covariate_only = B3$DIC, graph_only = C3$DIC)
table(PxG = A3$Label, truth = sim3$z)
table(covariate_only = B3$Label, truth = sim3$z)
table(graph_only = C3$Label, truth = sim3$z)
```

PxG recovers the two groups exactly; the covariate-only model splits one group, and the
graph-only model splits the other (paper Figure 7). The authors' call, which takes a few
minutes, is:

```{r ex3-fit, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(2022)
A3 <- PxG_PL(YData = sim3$Y, XData = sim3$X, spike = 0.01, slab = 5, a1 = 1, a2 = 1, alphaG = 0.1,
             mu0 = rep(0, 10), sigsq0 = 1, b1 = 1, b2 = 0.1, M = 1, N = 3,
             burnin = 500, nmcmc = 1000, z0 = sample(1:3, 500, TRUE), B = 1)   # DIC 104164.7
```

A short live chain already separates the groups:

```{r ex3-live}
set.seed(2022)
A3_short <- PxG_PL(YData = sim3$Y, XData = sim3$X, spike = 0.01, slab = 5, a1 = 1, a2 = 1, alphaG = 0.1,
                   mu0 = rep(0, 10), sigsq0 = 1, b1 = 1, b2 = 0.1, M = 1, N = 3,
                   burnin = 20, nmcmc = 50, z0 = sample(1:3, 500, TRUE), B = 1, verbose = FALSE)
table(A3_short$Label, sim3$z)
```

Figure 8 shows the per-cluster graphs estimated by `Graph_NS` on the recovered clusters
(saved in `Example3AG.RData`; `spike = 0.01`, `slab = 5`, `alphaG = 0.05`, 100 burn-in and
500 kept iterations), with true edges marked:

```{r ex3-fig8, fig.height = 4.5, fig.width = 9}
AG <- load_sup("Example3AG.RData")
G_est <- list(symmetrize_graph(AG$AG1), symmetrize_graph(AG$AG2))
truth <- list(sim3$G1, sim3$G2)
# the authors' label 2 is true cluster 1 and label 3 is true cluster 2
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3, 3, 2.5, 1))
for (k in 1:2) {
  M <- G_est[[k]]; q <- nrow(M)
  image(1:q, 1:q, t(M[q:1, ]), col = gray(seq(1, 0, length.out = 64)), zlim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE,
        xlab = "", ylab = "", main = sprintf("Cluster %d: posterior edge probability", k))
  Tt <- truth[[k]]; diag(Tt) <- 0
  idx <- which(Tt == 1 & upper.tri(Tt), arr.ind = TRUE)
  hit <- M[idx] >= 0.5
  points(idx[, 2], q + 1 - idx[, 1], pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = ifelse(hit, "green3", "red"))
  points(idx[, 1], q + 1 - idx[, 2], pch = 16, cex = 0.7, col = ifelse(hit, "green3", "red"))
}
```

Green dots are true edges recovered at posterior probability 0.5, red dots true edges
missed. The competitors on this example (BM13, mSSL and JRNS, Figure 9) are in
`vignette("competitors")`.
